note.explanation: Matter may be an element, a compound, or a mixture. An element has one kind of atom; a compound contains different elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio; a mixture contains substances mixed in any ratio.
examples: Salt water is a homogeneous mixture because its concentration is uniform throughout.
A sample of rock is a heterogeneous mixture because its constituents are not present in the same concentration throughout.
note.checkAnswer: A compound is a pure substance made up of two or more different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
note.simple: Think of the three types this way: an element has one kind of atom, a compound has different elements chemically joined, and a mixture has substances physically mixed together.
note.checkQuestion: What makes a compound different from a mixture?

steps: Check whether the sample contains one kind of atom, different elements chemically combined, or substances mixed together.

explain.title: Element
explain.body: Element is the simplest form of matter. It is a pure substance containing the same kind of atoms. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical reactions.

explain.title: Compound
explain.body: Compound is also a pure substance. It is made up of two or more different chemically elements combined in a fixed ratio. When elements come together, they react with each other and form chemical bonds that are not easy to break.

explain.title: Mixture
explain.body: A mixture is formed when more than one types of elements or compounds are mixed together in any ratio. A mixture may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

explain.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures
explain.body: A homogeneous mixture has uniform concentration throughout, as in salt water. A heterogeneous mixture has different concentrations of its constituents in different parts, as in a sample of rock.

mistakes: Do not call a compound a mixture: elements in a compound are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Do not say a mixture has to have a fixed ratio; its substances may be mixed in any ratio.
Do not classify a sample as homogeneous just because it contains several substances; check whether its composition is uniform throughout.
Do not say an element can be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical reactions.
